summary: Ranibizumab is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody fragment (Fab) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitor administered by intravitreal injection for retinal vascular diseases. It binds active forms of VEGF-A, preventing receptor binding and reducing pathologic angiogenesis, vascular leakage, and edema. Because it is delivered directly into the eye by an ophthalmologist, its principal safety concerns are ocular: endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, and increases in intraocular pressure.
indications: Macular edema following retinal vein occlusion (RVO)

dosage.d: 0.5 mg (0.05 mL of 10 mg/mL solution) once a month
dosage.t: Monthly; some patients may be maintained with less frequent dosing after initial loading
dosage.n: Administered by an ophthalmologist using aseptic technique

dosage.n: Each vial is for treatment of a single eye

admin: For ophthalmic intravitreal injection only; administered by a qualified ophthalmologist
Use aseptic technique with sterile gloves, sterile drape, and sterile eyelid speculum
Adequate anesthesia and a broad-spectrum microbicide should be given prior to injection
Withdraw the dose through a sterile filter needle, then inject with a 30-gauge injection needle
Monitor intraocular pressure before and within 60 minutes after injection (tonometry)
Each single-use vial or prefilled syringe is for treatment of one eye only
moa: Ranibizumab binds to the receptor binding site of the active forms of vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A), including the biologically active, cleaved form (VEGF110). This prevents the interaction of VEGF-A with its receptors (VEGFR1 and VEGFR2) on the surface of endothelial cells, thereby reducing endothelial cell proliferation, vascular leakage, and new blood vessel formation that drive neovascular eye disease and macular edema.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to ranibizumab or any of the excipients
monitor: Perfusion of the optic nerve head after injection
Signs of endophthalmitis or retinal detachment

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of ranibizumab administration in pregnant women. Animal reproduction studies showed a low incidence of skeletal abnormalities at intravitreal doses approximately 13 times the predicted human exposure. Systemic exposure after intravitreal injection is very low. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: There are no data on the presence of ranibizumab in human milk, its effects on the breastfed infant, or on milk production. Because many drugs are excreted in human milk and because of the potential for absorption and harm to infant growth and development, caution should be exercised when administering to a nursing woman.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is required for renal impairment. Systemic exposure following intravitreal administration is extremely low (serum concentrations are predicted to be roughly 90,000-fold lower than vitreal concentrations), so renal clearance is not a meaningful determinant of dosing.
hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment is required for hepatic impairment. Because intravitreal administration produces minimal systemic exposure, hepatic metabolism is not a significant factor in dosing.

major: No formal drug-drug interaction studies have been performed; clinically significant systemic interactions are not expected due to minimal systemic exposure
moderate: Concomitant intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy in the same eye (avoid; not studied)
minor: Other ophthalmic medications administered to the same eye (separate administration and observe sterile technique)
interactions.food: Not applicable; ranibizumab is administered as an intravitreal injection, not orally
interactions.alcohol: No known interaction with alcohol for this ophthalmic agent
interactions.diagnostics: No known interference with laboratory tests; transient post-injection intraocular pressure elevation may affect tonometry readings

common: Foreign body sensation in the eye
emergency: Sudden eye pain, redness, light sensitivity, or vision loss after injection (possible endophthalmitis or retinal detachment) - seek ophthalmologic care immediately
Signs of stroke or heart attack

counsel: This medication is given as an injection into the eye by your eye doctor; you will not self-administer it
In the days after the injection, report any eye pain, increasing redness, light sensitivity, blurred vision, or worsening vision immediately
Mild redness, floaters, or a feeling of something in the eye can occur and usually resolve
Keep all scheduled injection and monitoring appointments, as treatment is typically given on a regular monthly schedule
Do not rub or apply pressure to the treated eye
pk: Reduction in retinal edema and improvement in vision typically seen within the first weeks of monthly therapy
Mean maximum serum concentration about 1.7 ng/mL after a 0.5 mg intravitreal dose; vitreous peak occurs locally at injection
Estimated average vitreous elimination half-life approximately 9 days
Effect supports a monthly intravitreal dosing interval
Refrigerate at 2-8 C (36-46 F); do not freeze; protect from light
pearls: Delivered by intravitreal injection by an ophthalmologist; never self-administered
Two strengths exist: 0.5 mg (10 mg/mL) for AMD, RVO, and mCNV, and 0.3 mg (6 mg/mL) for DME and DR
Endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, and increased intraocular pressure are the key procedural risks - monitor IOP before and after injection
Systemic exposure is minimal, so renal and hepatic adjustments are not needed
Each vial or prefilled syringe treats a single eye only to prevent contamination
missed: Ranibizumab is not a home medication and cannot be self-administered. If an injection appointment is missed, contact the ophthalmology clinic promptly to reschedule, since the regimen relies on timely (often monthly) dosing to maintain disease control. Do not attempt to make up doses on your own.
overdose: More concentrated doses as high as 2 mg of ranibizumab in 0.05 mL have been administered to patients without additional unexpected adverse reactions. Inadvertent overdose may increase the risk of elevated intraocular pressure; management is supportive with monitoring and treatment of IOP and any intraocular inflammation.
